cues.en: So I will start by pointing out that the giant AT&T cell mask that's over there is because of Southby. And so like most things in Austin right now, the problem with the microphone today is Southby's fault. So thanks for that intro, Mary. That was very kind. You're always way too kind. I really appreciate it. I really love what Mary and Ruth and the whole team at White October have built in this event. I think it's something that those of us that care deeply about leading well...
cues.zh: 我先说明一下，那边那个巨大的AT&T广告牌是Southby搞的。所以就像奥斯汀现在的大多数事情一样，今天麦克风的问题也是Southby的锅。谢谢你刚才的介绍，Mary，你太客气了，你总是太客气了，我真的很感激。我真的很喜欢Mary、Ruth以及White October整个团队打造的这个活动。我觉得这正是我们这些深切关心如何做好领导的人……

cues.en: Really needed and so I'm thankful it exists in the world. So thank you for all the time and effort and attention that you put into it I'm especially excited and thankful. Yeah, please I'm especially excited and thankful that they brought it to my hometown of Austin and I am incredibly honored to be on this stage tonight So when I was a kid my parents gave me this four volume set of books called how things work My dad is a mechanical engineer by training and I think the reason they gave me this set of books is because he got tired of answering all of my complicated questions about
cues.zh: 真正需要的，所以我很庆幸它存在于这个世界上。感谢你们投入的所有时间、精力和关注，我特别激动也特别感激。对，请讲，我特别激动也特别感激他们把这个活动带到了我的家乡奥斯汀，今晚能站在这个舞台上我无比荣幸。小时候，我父母给了我一套四卷本的书，叫《事物如何运作》。我爸爸是科班出身的机械工程师，我想他们给我这套书的原因，是他厌倦了回答我所有关于……

cues.en: how things work. Maybe it was that, maybe it was that he wanted to teach me to get these answers on my own. I don't have a chance to look at these books very often these days, but they still occupy a treasured spot on my bookshelf because they're a big part of what made me who I am. I think these books are a big part of why I'm interested in all these weird disasters and the stories that I like to tell. I distinctly remember when it was all over the local news in 1990 that Comanche Peak Unit 1 outside of Dallas had gone online.
cues.zh: 事物如何运作的复杂问题。也许是这样，也许是他想教会我自己去寻找这些答案。现在我不常有机会翻这些书了，但它们依然在我书架上占据着一个珍贵的位置，因为它们在很大程度上塑造了今天的我。我觉得这些书很大程度上解释了为什么我对这些稀奇古怪的灾难、以及我喜欢讲的那些故事感兴趣。我清楚地记得，1990年当地新闻都在报道达拉斯郊外的科曼奇峰1号机组并网发电了。

cues.en: was the first nuclear reactor that I remember hearing about. And I remember turning here to pages 68 and 69 of volume 1 of how things work to try to make sense of how a nuclear reactor made electricity. And I think that's a good place for us to start today as well with one of the reactor diagrams at the bottom of this page. As it turns out, the basic mechanics of a nuclear power plant are the same as a combustion power plant. A heat source heats up water. In this case, it's a carefully controlled nuclear reaction fueled by uranium, but in a...
cues.zh: 这是我记忆中听说过的第一座核反应堆。我记得翻到《万物运作原理》第1卷第68和69页，想弄明白核反应堆是如何发电的。我觉得今天我们也从那页底部的反应堆示意图开始讲起，是个不错的起点。实际上，核电站的基本原理和燃烧发电厂是一样的。一个热源把水加热。在这个例子里，是铀燃料驱动的、受到精心控制的核反应，但在一个……

cues.en: In a combustion plant, it would be burning coal or natural gas, and that heat heats up water. High-pressure water circulating through the reactor carries the heat to a heat exchanger, where it's used to boil water, turning it into steam. Steam gets piped to the turbine, which is basically a giant fan in a tube, and the turbine turns a generator, and that's what finally produces the electricity. After that, the steam gets pumped into a condenser, where it gets cooled and turned back into water, and around and around it goes. So what exactly makes this...
cues.zh: 在燃烧发电厂里，烧的是煤或天然气，那份热量把水加热。高压水在反应堆中循环，把热量带到热交换器，在那里把水煮沸，变成蒸汽。蒸汽通过管道送到涡轮机，涡轮机基本上就是管子里的一个巨型风扇，涡轮机带动发电机，最终就产生了电。之后，蒸汽被泵入冷凝器，冷却后重新变成水，就这样循环往复。那么，到底是什么让这个……

cues.en: a pressurized water reactor because that's important for us to understand today. The components I just walked you through are on two separate coolant circulation loops. There's a primary loop in orange here that consists of the water that flows through the reactor vessel to gather the heat and then through the heat exchanger over and over again. That's the only place that water goes. And then there's a secondary loop here in blue that flows through the heat exchanger where it boils into steam.
cues.zh: 压水反应堆，因为这对我们今天的理解很重要。我刚才带大家看的那些部件分布在两个独立的冷却剂循环回路上。这里橙色的是一回路，由流经反应堆压力容器收集热量、再反复流经热交换器的水组成。那水只去这一个地方。然后这里蓝色的二回路，流经热交换器，在那里沸腾成蒸汽。

cues.en: and the expansion of that steam is what drives the turbine to generate the electricity, and then it's condensed back into water, and it goes through that secondary loop over and over again. These two loops never mix, they're completely isolated, the water is completely separate. And the thing that makes it a pressurized water reactor is that the primary loop is held at about 2,000 psi, and there's a very simple economic reason for this.
cues.zh: 蒸汽膨胀驱动汽轮机发电，然后冷凝回水，再反复流经那个二次回路。这两个回路从不混合，完全隔离，水也完全分开。而它之所以是压水反应堆，是因为主回路维持在约2000 psi，这有个非常简单的经济原因。

cues.en: So a boiling water reactor, the other major type of nuclear reactor, has to have a very large reactor pressure vessel, because the water actually boils to steam in the reactor itself. There has to be room for that expansion to take place. The reactor vessel in a pressurized reactor can be much smaller, because when you raise the pressure of water, it raises the boiling point. And so the water in the primary loop is about 600 degrees Fahrenheit, but because it's held at such high pressure, it doesn't boil. Or at least it shouldn't.
cues.zh: 沸水反应堆是另一种主要核反应堆类型，它必须有非常大的反应堆压力容器，因为水在反应堆本身内就沸腾成蒸汽。必须留出空间让这种膨胀发生。压水反应堆的反应堆容器可以小得多，因为提高水的压力会提高沸点。所以主回路中的水约600华氏度，但由于压力如此之高，它不会沸腾。至少本不该沸腾。

cues.en: And that brings us to March 28, 1979. Three Mile Island Nuclear Generating Station is a two-unit nuclear power plant in Londonderry Township, Pennsylvania. It's built on a three-mile-long sandbar in the middle of the Susquehanna River, and it's about 10 miles south of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, the capital of the state. Unit 1 is an 820-megawatt Babcock & Wilcox pressurized water reactor that began commercial operation on September 2, 1974.
cues.zh: 这就把我们带到1979年3月28日。三里岛核电站是宾夕法尼亚州伦敦德里镇的一座双机组核电厂。它建在萨斯奎哈纳河中央一个三英里长的沙洲上，位于宾夕法尼亚州首府哈里斯堡以南约10英里。1号机组是一座820兆瓦的Babcock & Wilcox压水反应堆，于1974年9月2日开始商业运行。

cues.en: On March 28, it's been operating for about five years, no incidents, and it's currently offline for refueling outages. This reactor is not operating. Unit 2 is also a Babcock & Wilcox pressurized water reactor. It's slightly larger, 906 megawatts, and it went into commercial operation on December 30, 1978, which, if you do the math, it's only three months old at this point. This reactor has only been running for three months on the morning of March 28, 1979.
cues.zh: 3月28日，它已经运行了大约五年，没有发生任何事故，目前因换料大修而停机。这座反应堆并未运行。2号机组同样是一座巴布科克·威尔科克斯压水反应堆。它的功率稍大一些，为906兆瓦，于1978年12月30日投入商业运行——算一下就知道，到此时它才运行了三个月。1979年3月28日早晨，这座反应堆才刚运行了三个月。

cues.en: And on that morning, it's running at 97% of max capacity. It's running hot, straight, and normal, as they say in the nuclear power industry. These four men are at the controls of Three Mile Island Unit 2 for the overnight shift on March 28. Bill Zewe is the shift supervisor for Units 1 and 2. He's the most senior person on site for the overnight shift. Fred Shimon is the shift foreman for Unit 2. He's Bill Zewe's second in command.
cues.zh: 那天早上，它以最大功率的97%运行着。用核电行业的话说，它运行得火热、平稳、正常。这四个人在3月28日值夜班，负责三哩岛2号机组的控制。Bill Zewe是1号和2号机组的值班主管。他是夜班期间现场级别最高的人。Fred Shimon是2号机组的值班领班。他是Bill Zewe的副手。

cues.en: These two gentlemen on the end, Ed Frederick and Craig Faust, are the control room operators on duty. They're the ones that are actually sitting at the controls in the reactor control room. Everything at the plant was going perfectly normal that night. The plant was running exactly as designed except for a small problem in the condensate polisher that the swing shift the night before had left them to deal with. What are condensate polishers? They are a set in Three Mile Island, a set of eight filtration tanks that filter the water.
cues.zh: 末端的这两位先生，Ed Frederick和Craig Faust，是当班的控制室操作员。他们才是真正坐在反应堆控制室控制台前的人。那天晚上，电厂的一切都完全正常。电厂完全按设计运行，只是凝结水精处理装置有个小问题，是前一晚中班留下来让他们处理的。什么是凝结水精处理装置？在三哩岛，它是一组八个过滤水箱，用来过滤水。

cues.en: in the secondary coolant loop coming out of the condenser before it goes back into the expensive and delicate steam generators. And these are not the actual condensate polishers from 3 Mile Island. As you can imagine, it's very difficult to find a picture of a specific component of a specific nuclear power plant. But this is what they look like. And these polishers are filled with sticky resin beads. And what these beads do is anything that might be in the water that's not water, like little flecks of rust or dust or whatever, they stick to these resin beads.
cues.zh: 位于冷凝器流出的二回路冷却循环中，之后水会重新流入昂贵且娇贵的蒸汽发生器。这并不是 3 Mile Island 当时的真实凝结水精处理器。你可以想象，要找到某个特定核电站具体部件的照片有多难。但它们大概就长这样。这些精处理器里面装满了有粘性的树脂颗粒。这些颗粒的作用是，水中一旦有除水以外的任何杂质，比如细小的锈斑或灰尘之类的，都会吸附在这些树脂颗粒上。

cues.en: The only problem with this system is that as the 5,000 tons of water that pass through these tanks push on these beads, they tend to compress. And the problem that the crew was facing this night is that the beads in the number seven polisher tank had completely clogged the tank. So the crew on the swing shift had started working on this problem. These tanks have a backwash system that works about like a pool filter backwash. So they had used that. It wasn't sufficient. So they had turned on a compressed air feed as well, feeding compressed air into the tank.
cues.zh: 这套系统唯一的问题是，随着 5000 吨水穿过这些罐体压迫这些颗粒，颗粒往往会被压缩紧实。当晚工作人员面临的问题是，7 号精处理罐里的颗粒把罐子彻底堵死了。于是中班的工作人员开始着手解决这个问题。这些罐体配有反冲洗系统，原理和泳池过滤器的反冲洗差不多。他们用了这个方法，但不够管用。所以他们还开启了压缩空气补气装置，向罐内注入压缩空气。

cues.en: At 3.59 in the morning, Fred Shimon is down in the basement of the turbine hall to see how things are coming, to see if this tank is unstuck yet. He's looking in the viewing port of the number seven tank when things get incredibly quiet. You can imagine that 5,000 tons of water per hour moving makes a tremendous amount of noise, so the sudden quiet is very disconcerting. And he barely jumps free before a water hammer comes through and actually dislodges the feed pipe feeding all eight of these condensate polisher tanks. Now, what had happened is...
cues.zh: 凌晨 3 点 59 分，Fred Shimon 来到汽轮机房地下室查看进展，看看这个罐子到底通了没有。他正透过 7 号罐的视窗往里看，周围突然变得异常安静。你可以想象，每小时 5000 吨水奔流会产生极大的噪音，所以这突如其来的安静让人心里发毛。他刚勉强跳开躲避，一道水锤就猛冲过来，生生震脱了供给这全部八个凝结水精处理罐的进水管。那么，当时到底发生了什么呢……

cues.en: Over the last 10 hours or so, a leaky one-way check valve had allowed water to press up from in the condensate polisher tank into the air feed line. And over the course of 10 hours, it had worked its way all the way up to the manifold that fed all eight of the pneumatic control valves that controlled the inlets for these condensate polishers. And so all eight of these tanks closed off at the same time. Obviously, this is not good. But to help us understand why, here is a schematic of Three Mile Island Unit 2.
cues.zh: 在过去大约 10 个小时里，一个泄漏的单向止回阀让水从凝结水精处理器水箱向上顶入空气供给管线。经过这 10 个小时，水一路上升到歧管，而这个歧管向控制这 些凝结水精处理器入口的 8 个气动控制阀供气。于是，这 8 个水箱同时关闭了。显然，这可不是什么好事。为了帮助我们理解其中的原因，先来看一张三里岛核电站 2 号机组的示意图。

cues.en: Looks a little more complicated than the diagram we looked at a minute ago, but I've got it colored the same as that schematic. The primary loop's in orange, secondary loop is in blue. Let me get you oriented real quick. Here in the center is the reactor vessel, where the nuclear chain reaction creates heat. Next to it are the two steam generators, what the other diagram called the heat exchanger, where heat from the primary loop boils water in the secondary loop to create steam. This is a critical component of the plant, so there's two of them for redundancy.
cues.zh: 看起来比我们刚才看的那张图复杂一些，但我给它用了和那张示意图相同的配色。一回路是橙色，二回路是蓝色。我先快速帮大家熟悉一下方位。中间这里是反应堆压力容器，核链式反应就在这里产生热量。旁边是两个蒸汽发生器，也就是另一张图中所说的热交换器。一回路的热量在这里把二回路中的水烧成蒸汽。这是电站的关键部件，所以设置了两个，以实现冗余。

cues.en: That steam generated in the steam generators is piped to the turbine building to turn the turbine and generator. And then here's the condenser where the steam cools down and gets cooled enough to change back into water. One interesting tidbit that I'll point out. Most people think that this cooling tower is a nuclear reactor. It's actually not. It's the little tiny building that's next to the cooling tower. And here, right after the condensate polisher, right after the condenser is the condensate polisher. And so with the condensate polisher section completely blocked,
cues.zh: 蒸汽发生器产生的蒸汽通过管道输送到汽轮机厂房，带动汽轮机和发电机。这里是冷凝器，蒸汽在这里冷却，最终重新变回水。我顺便指出一个有意思的小知识：大多数人以为这个冷却塔就是核反应堆，其实不是。核反应堆是旁边那栋很小的建筑。这里，在凝结水精处理器的后面，也就是冷凝器的后面，就是凝结水精处理器。而随着凝结水精处理器这一段完全堵塞，

cues.en: There is no more water to be pumped through the secondary cooling loop, and so the main feedwater pump trips offline. It's 36 seconds past four in the morning, the official start of the accident at Three Mile Island. Two seconds after the main feedwater pumps trip, the turbine senses it's not going to be getting any more steam, and so it trips offline along with the generator. When this happens, the plant's got a bunch of steam that it no longer needs, so the main safety valves of the plant open and release a ton of steam into the early morning sky.
cues.zh: 二回路中就再也没有水可以继续泵送了，于是主给水泵跳闸停机。现在是凌晨 4 点过 36 秒，这就是三里岛事故正式开始的时间。主给水泵跳闸两秒后，汽轮机检测到自己将不再获得蒸汽，于是也随同发电机一起跳闸停机。这时，电站里有大量不再需要的蒸汽，于是电站的主安全阀打开，将大量蒸汽释放到清晨的天空中。

cues.en: It's harmless, it's not radioactive, but it makes a ton of noise. It can be heard from miles away. In the control room, Ed Frederick and Craig Faust are getting their first indications that something has gone awry. An alarm horn is sounding, announcing that the turbine has tripped offline, and several alarm indicators start to flash. A few seconds after the turbine and generator alarms go off, the pressure in the reactor vessel is starting to climb rapidly. Now, this is not unexpected. You see, with no water in the secondary loop, the heat that's built up in the primary coolant loop has nowhere to go.
cues.zh: 它本身无害，没有放射性，但会发出巨大的噪音，几英里外都能听到。在控制室里，Ed Frederick 和 Craig Faust 第一次察觉到有些不对劲。警报喇叭响了起来，宣布汽轮机已跳闸脱网，几个报警指示灯开始闪烁。汽轮机和发电机警报响起几秒后，反应堆压力容器内的压力开始迅速攀升。不过这并不意外。要知道，二回路里没有水，一回路冷却剂中积聚的热量就无处可去。

cues.en: And when water heats up, it expands, and so it's normal that with nowhere for the heat to go, the pressure's going to go up. The good news is that the plant is designed for exactly this scenario, and as soon as that alarm went off, it began taking action to resolve the situation automatically. The reactor's pressure control system is the first to jump into action. Now, there are two components to this system, and both of them are important to the accident. The first one we're going to talk about is the pressurizer. Now, the pressurizer's main job is to maintain system pressure.
cues.zh: 水受热会膨胀，所以热量无处可去时压力升高是正常现象。好消息是，核电站的设计恰好覆盖了这种场景，警报一响，电站就开始自动采取措施来解决问题。反应堆的压力控制系统第一个投入行动。这个系统有两个组成部分，它们都与这次事故密切相关。我们要讲的第一个是稳压器。稳压器的主要职责，是维持加压核反应堆的系统压力。

cues.en: in a pressurized nuclear reactor, and this works like a giant piston. The red area at the top is steam, and the blue at the bottom is liquid water. Now, water expands when it gets hot, like I just said, so when they need to raise the pressure of the system, there's a heating element at the bottom that they can turn on, and that'll raise the pressure in the entire primary coolant loop. When they need to lower the pressure, there's a sprayer at the top they can turn on, and by lowering the pressure in the pressurizer, it'll lower the pressure of the entire system. But there's a couple other purposes that the pressurizer serves as well.
cues.zh: 它的工作原理就像一个巨大的活塞。顶部的红色区域是蒸汽，底部的蓝色是液态水。正如刚才所说，水受热会膨胀，所以当需要升高系统压力时，可以打开底部的一个加热元件，它就会提高整个一回路冷却剂的压力。需要降压时，可以打开顶部的一个喷淋装置，通过降低稳压器内的压力，来降低整个系统的压力。不过稳压器还有其他几个作用。

cues.en: Babcock and Wilcox designed this particular nuclear reactor without any water-level monitoring in the reactor vessel itself. The reason for this is because the pressurizer is the highest point in the system. And so, if you monitor the water in the pressurizer, you can infer that if there's water there, there's water in the reactor vessel. And it was much cheaper to put instrumentation in the pressurizer than the reactor vessel itself where it's exposed to high radioactivity. And the third job that the pressurizer does is it absorbs pressure shocks.
cues.zh: Babcock and Wilcox在设计这座核反应堆时，反应堆压力容器本身没有配备任何水位监测装置。原因在于稳压器是系统中最高的点。所以，只要监测稳压器中的水位，就能推断出：如果稳压器里有水，反应堆压力容器里也就有水。而且，在稳压器中安装仪表的成本要低得多，因为反应堆压力容器本身暴露在高放射性环境下。稳压器的第三项功能是吸收压力冲击。

cues.en: Steam is significantly more compressible than water. And so, the steam bubble at the top of the pressurizer acts as a giant shock absorber when the system experiences a significant quick pressure increase, much like it's experiencing right now. So the steam in the pressurizer absorbs the initial shock, but the pressurizer is designed for small, fine pressure adjustments. Right now, the primary loop is at 2,250 PSI, about 100 PSI over operating pressure, and it would take the pressurizer a few minutes to make that much of an adjustment.
cues.zh: 蒸汽的可压缩性明显高于水。因此，当系统经历剧烈的快速压力上升时——就像它现在正在经历的那样——稳压器顶部的蒸汽泡就像一个巨大的减震器。稳压器中的蒸汽会吸收最初的冲击，但稳压器的设计初衷只是做小幅、精细的压力调节。目前，主回路压力为2250 PSI，比运行压力高出约100 PSI，而稳压器需要几分钟才能完成这么大的调节量。

cues.en: So what does the system do to deal with a big pressure change like this one? Well, that's where the pilot-operated relief valve comes in. And if you've ever heard the story of Three Mile Island Unit 2, this is the component that you probably remember because it's the one that gets all of the press. In the event of a big pressure spike, the pilot-operated relief valve will open, and it will release coolant into a drain tank on the containment building floor. The PORV opens four seconds after the turbine and generator trip offline. A few seconds later...
cues.zh: 那么，系统如何应对这样大的压力变化呢？这就是先导式安全阀发挥作用的地方。如果你听过三哩岛2号机组的故事，这大概就是你记得的那个部件，因为它承受了所有的舆论压力。在发生大幅压力尖峰时，先导式安全阀会打开，将冷却剂排放到安全壳建筑地面上的排水箱中。汽轮机和发电机跳闸离线四秒后，PORV打开。几秒钟后……

cues.en: The computer senses that even with the PORV open, pressure in the reactor vessel is still continuing to rise, so it takes another defensive reaction. It scrams the reactor. Now, the chain reaction in the core of a nuclear reactor consists of a bunch of neutrons bouncing around, running into uranium atoms, and causing them to fission or split. When that happens, it gives off a tremendous amount of heat and a bunch more neutrons that then go off and crash into other uranium atoms, continuing the chain reaction.
cues.zh: 计算机检测到即使PORV打开，反应堆容器内的压力仍在持续上升，于是采取另一防御措施：紧急停堆。核反应堆堆芯的链式反应，是一群中子四处弹跳、撞上铀原子、使其裂变或分裂的过程。裂变时释放巨大热量和更多中子，这些中子再去撞击其他铀原子，维持链式反应。

cues.en: The way that you control this chain reaction is via a set of cadmium rods that can be inserted into the reactor core. What they do is they absorb these neutrons and keep them from flying into uranium atoms. When the reactor scrams, what happens is the control mechanism that is responsible for lowering and raising these pressure rods releases them, and they freefall to the bottom of the reactor core. And this stops the nuclear chain reaction almost instantly. But even after the scram, the reactor core is still producing decay heat.
cues.zh: 控制链式反应的方法，是用一组可插入堆芯的镉棒。镉棒吸收中子，阻止它们飞向铀原子。紧急停堆时，负责升降这些控制棒的控制机构释放它们，控制棒自由落体到堆芯底部，几乎瞬间中止核链式反应。但紧急停堆后，堆芯仍在产生衰变热。

cues.en: Immediately after a scram, it's producing about 6.5% of whatever it was producing before it was scrambled. An hour later, it's producing 1.5%. So it's incredibly critical that cooling is maintained for the core throughout this first hour, because that's plenty of heat that if it's not carried away, if it accumulates in the core, it can cause significant damage. A few seconds later, back in the control room, a light on the console turns from red to green to indicate that the pilot-operated relief valve has closed. At this point, everything feels very much under control with the reactor operators.
cues.zh: 紧急停堆后瞬间，衰变热约为停堆前功率的6.5%，一小时后降至1.5%。因此，这第一小时内必须维持堆芯冷却，否则热量积聚在堆芯会造成严重损坏。几秒后，控制室控制台上一盏灯由红变绿，表示先导式安全阀已关闭。此时，反应堆操作员感觉一切尽在掌控。

cues.en: Reactor and turbine trips, they're not an everyday occurrence because obviously you want the plant to stay online and generate electricity, but they're also not an emergency. They're well-established procedures for responding to them. The alarm horns are still blaring, the alarm medicators are still flashing, but the system is behaving exactly as it's designed. That feeling of control for the reactor operators would last for precisely two minutes. Because two minutes later, the emergency core cooling system turns on.
cues.zh: 反应堆和汽轮机跳闸，这并非日常事件，因为显然你希望核电站保持在线发电，但它们也不是紧急情况。应对这些有成熟的规程。警报声仍在刺耳响起，警报指示器仍在闪烁，但系统正完全按设计运行。反应堆操作员的这种掌控感只持续了恰恰两分钟。因为两分钟后，应急堆芯冷却系统启动了。

cues.en: specifically the high-pressure injection pumps, dumping 1,000 gallons per minute of cold water straight into the reactor core. The plant had gone from a state they understood to one they didn't as soon as the high-pressure injection turned on. The reason this confused them so much is because they were watching the water level in the pressurizer, and the water level in the pressurizer was rising. Seeing the water level in the pressurizer rise told them that there was plenty of water in the system, so they couldn't understand why the high-pressure injection system thought the system needed more water.
cues.zh: 具体来说，高压注入泵每分钟将1000加仑的冷水直接注入反应堆堆芯。高压注入一启动，核电站就从他们理解的状态变成了他们不理解的状态。让他们如此困惑的原因是，他们一直在观察稳压器中的水位，而稳压器中的水位在上升。看到稳压器水位上升告诉他们系统中有充足的水，所以他们无法理解为什么高压注入系统认为系统需要更多水。

cues.en: And so, Fred Scheman made the call to turn off the high-pressure injection system after it had only been running for about two and a half minutes. Had he not done that, had he just left it alone, let it do its job, this would have been a minor inconvenience and this plant would have been back online about two days after this incident. We're now five minutes into the accident sequence. There's something at this point that's perplexing Bill Zewie. He's the one that you can kind of see hunched over in the paisley shirt right in the middle. The water level in the pressurizer is continuing to rise.
cues.zh: 于是，Fred Scheman 决定在高压注入系统仅运行了约两分半钟后就将其关闭。如果他没有这样做，如果他放手不管，让它发挥作用，这本来只会是个小麻烦，核电站会在事故发生后大约两天恢复运行。现在事故序列已经进行了五分钟。此时有件事让 Bill Zewie 困惑不解。他就是中间那个你能看到穿着佩斯利花纹衬衫弓着身子的人。稳压器中的水位继续上升。

cues.en: So he knows the primary loop is full of water, but the pressure of the primary loop is continuing to drop. And this is a problem because if it drops too far, the water in the primary loop is going to start to boil, and it won't be able to cool the fuel rods. So he has a hunch of what's going on. He suspects that maybe the pilot-operated relief valve might be stuck open. And that's why the system's having trouble maintaining pressure. So he double-checks the pilot-operated relief valve indicator on the control panel. It still shows close, just as it did before.
cues.zh: 他知道主回路里满是水，但主回路的压力还在持续下降。这是个问题，因为如果压力降得太低，主回路里的水就会开始沸腾，就无法冷却燃料棒了。所以他心里对情况有了猜测。他怀疑 pilot-operated relief valve（先导式卸压阀）可能卡在了开启状态。这就是系统难以维持压力的原因。于是他又核对了一下控制面板上 pilot-operated relief valve 的指示器。它仍然显示关闭，和之前一样。

cues.en: Just to make sure, he has one of the reactor operators check the outlet temperature of the pilot-operated relief valve. The reading comes back at 228 degrees Fahrenheit. This seems perfectly normal to Bill Zewie, so he moves on. There's a problem with that decision, though. The plant operation manual indicates that any reading over 200 degrees Fahrenheit indicates that the pilot-operated relief valve is open. And if that's the case, then the manual block valve in front of it should be closed to prevent coolant from leaking out of the system.
cues.zh: 为了确认，他让一位反应堆操作员去检查 pilot-operated relief valve 的出口温度。读数回来是 228 华氏度。这在 Bill Zewie 看来完全正常，于是他就继续往下走了。但这个判断有问题。电厂操作手册指出，任何超过 200 华氏度的读数都表明 pilot-operated relief valve 是开启的。而如果是这样，那么它前面的手动隔离阀就应该关闭，以防止冷却剂从系统中泄漏出去。

cues.en: Had Bill Zewie just closed the block valve, he would have stopped the accident right then and there. But he doesn't. He leaves it open. We're now six minutes into the accident. Five minutes later, at 4.11 a.m., another alarm goes off. This one indicates that the sump in the containment building is filling up. The sump is a pit at the bottom of the containment building that collects any water that might leak or be vented from somewhere in the system. In this case, what's happening is that so much water has come out of the pilot-operated relief valve,
cues.zh: 要是 Bill Zewie 当时关掉那个隔离阀，他本可以当场就制止这场事故。但他没有。他让它保持开启。现在事故已经过去了六分钟。五分钟后，也就是凌晨 4 点 11 分，另一个警报响了。这个警报表明安全壳建筑里的集水坑正在积水。集水坑是安全壳建筑底部的一个坑，用来收集系统某处可能泄漏或排出的水。在这个情况下，发生的是大量水从 pilot-operated relief valve 流出，

cues.en: from the primary coolant loop that has filled up the drain tank on the floor of the containment building, and the drain tank has started overflowing into the sump. Now, enough water to fill up the sump at the bottom of the containment building should have told these guys that they had a giant leak, but they miss it. They don't catch that clue. The core is in serious trouble at this point, but the operators still aren't done. Just after 5 a.m., the floor of the control room starts to rumble. It's really subtle at first.
cues.zh: 从主冷却剂回路流出，灌满了安全壳建筑地面上的疏水箱，而疏水箱已经开始溢出到集水坑里。现在，积满安全壳建筑底部集水坑的水量本应告诉这些人，他们遇到了巨大的泄漏，但他们错过了。他们没有抓住这个线索。此时堆芯已经陷入严重麻烦，但操作员们还没完。刚过凌晨 5 点，控制室的地板开始震动。一开始非常轻微。

cues.en: but it quickly becomes impossible to ignore. What's happening is that the primary coolant pumps of the reactor are starting to vibrate because there's steam in the core, and the pumps are pushing around steam in addition to the water that they're designed to pump, and this is causing a lot of turbulence. And they know what their training says to do when this happens. In order to keep the very large, very expensive pumps from vibrating themselves to pieces and creating a coolant leak, they're supposed to be shut down.
cues.zh: 但它很快就变得无法忽视了。发生的情况是，反应堆的主冷却剂泵开始剧烈振动，因为堆芯里出现了蒸汽，泵除了原本设计要输送的水之外，还在推动蒸汽，这导致了大量的紊流。他们知道发生这种情况时培训手册是怎么要求的。为了防止这个非常巨大、非常昂贵的泵把自己振碎并造成冷却剂泄漏，理应将它们关闭。

cues.en: They hold out as long as they can because they're worried about what this might mean if they turn these pumps off, but 15 minutes in, Bill Zee, we can't stand it any longer, and he turns off the first set of pumps. This helps for a little while, but 30 minutes later, the vibration has gotten bad again, and he turns off the other set. It's now 544 in the morning, and this nuclear reactor that was running at 97% of max capacity less than two hours earlier now has no coolant being circulated through its core. None.
cues.zh: 他们尽可能地坚持着，因为他们担心关掉这些泵会意味着什么，但在15分钟后，比尔·齐（Bill Zee）实在无法忍受了，他关掉了第一组泵。这在短时间内起到了作用，但30分钟后，振动再次变得严重起来，他又关掉了另一组泵。现在是早上5点44分，这个不到两小时前还以最大功率97%运行的核反应堆，现在已经没有任何冷却剂在堆芯中循环了。一点也没有。

cues.en: It doesn't take very long for the effects of no circulation to make themselves known. At 6 a.m., precisely two hours into the accident, a radiation alarm like this one starts going off in the containment building. Now that tells us a couple things. The first, for a radiation alarm to be going off, one or more of these fuel rods has to have been damaged. Nuclear fuel is packaged in zirconium rods like this, and it's a bunch of uranium capsules that are about the size of your pinky.
cues.zh: 没有循环的后果很快就显现出来了。早上6点，事故发生正好两小时后，像这样的辐射警报开始在安全壳内拉响。这向我们透露了几件事。首先，既然辐射警报在响，说明这些燃料棒中有一根或多根已经受损。核燃料被打包在这样的锆棒中，里面是一堆大约你小指大小的铀胶囊。

cues.en: The beauty of this arrangement is that it keeps the radioactivity in the fuel rods from leaking into the primary coolant. So for them to be detecting radioactivity in the containment building, the rods have started to rupture. The other thing that tells us is if the fuel rods have been damaged, then it's almost certain that the water level in the reactor vessel has dropped below the top of the core. Now, by this point, plant leadership has started to make its way to the plant. Gary Miller is the station manager, the chief executive of Three Mile Island. This is his power plant.
cues.zh: 这种布局的好处在于，它能让燃料棒中的放射性物质不会泄漏到一回路冷却剂里。所以当他们在安全壳厂房内检测到放射性时，说明燃料棒已经开始破裂了。这还告诉我们的另一件事是：如果燃料棒已经受损，那么几乎可以肯定，反应堆压力容器里的水位已经降到堆芯顶部以下。到了这个时候，电厂的管理层已经开始赶往电厂。加里·米勒是站长，也就是三里岛的最高负责人。这是他的核电站。

cues.en: And George Cunder is the technical support manager for Three Mile Island Unit 2, so he manages all the technical specialists on staff, the nuclear engineers, the health physicists, the chemists. Almost as soon as they walk in the door, they're asked to join a conference call with Leland Rogers, a site rep for Babcock & Wilcox, the company that designed this reactor. And as these three guys are talking through what they know about the state of the plant, Rogers says, they closed the block valve, right? Block valve, the valve that Bill Zee, we decided not to close earlier.
cues.zh: 乔治·坎德是三里岛2号机组的技术支持经理，负责管理厂里所有的技术专家——核工程师、保健物理学家、化学家。他们几乎一进门，就被要求参加一个电话会议，与会者是利兰·罗杰斯，他是巴布科克·威尔科克斯公司——设计这座反应堆的公司——的驻厂代表。当这三个人在梳理他们所掌握的电厂状态信息时，罗杰斯问道：他们把隔离阀关上了，对吧？隔离阀，就是之前比尔·齐和我们决定不关的那个阀门。

cues.en: George Cunder in the control room yells at somebody else and says, is the block valve shut? A few seconds later, the answer comes back. Yeah, it's shut. And so at 6.22 in the morning, two hours and 22 minutes after the start of the accident, the block valve is finally closed, and the leak in the system is finally sealed. Now, had they done that 20 minutes into the accident, it would have been the right thing to do. At this point, it actually made things worse. And the reason for that is that this valve
cues.zh: 在控制室里的乔治·坎德冲着另一个人大喊：隔离阀关上了吗？几秒钟后，答复传来：是的，关上了。于是，在早上6点22分——事故发生两小时二十二分钟之后——隔离阀终于被关闭，系统里的泄漏终于被封住了。如果他们在事故发生20分钟时就这么做，那会是正确的操作。但到了这个时候，这反而让情况变得更糟了。原因在于，这个阀门

cues.en: was the only way that heat could escape from the reactor vessel in the primary coolant loop. The only way the core was keeping itself cool at this point was boiling off coolant and venting it out through the pilot-operated relief valve. So with the valve closed, the heat in the core intensified rapidly. It took about eight minutes for the top of the core to collapse. Subsequent calculations would show that by 7 a.m., the core was two-thirds uncovered,
cues.zh: 是热量从反应堆压力容器逃逸到一回路冷却剂回路的唯一途径。此时堆芯维持自身冷却的唯一方式，就是把冷却剂煮沸，再通过先导式泄压阀排放出去。所以阀门一关，堆芯里的热量迅速加剧。大约八分钟后，堆芯顶部就坍塌了。后续的计算表明，到早上7点，堆芯已有三分之二裸露在外，

cues.en: And temperatures in the hottest part of the core were about 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit, hot enough not only to melt the zirconium fuel rod cladding, but the uranium fuel inside as well. At 720 in the morning, the radiation alarm in the top of the containment building goes off, indicating a reading of 800 rem per hour.
cues.zh: 堆芯最热部分的温度约为4000华氏度，这个温度不仅足以熔化锆合金燃料棒包壳，连里面的铀燃料也能熔化。早上7点20分，安全壳厂房顶部的辐射警报响了，显示读数为每小时800雷姆。

cues.en: Now, to give you some context for what that means, if one of the operators from the plant had been standing in an 800-rim per hour field, they would have gotten their maximum yearly allowable dose of radiation in 20 seconds. The crew had largely been in denial about the state of the plant and core damage after the first radiation alarm went off. But when this one went off, this is the big one. Immediately after this alarm, they finally decide it's time to turn high-pressure injection back on. But they only leave it running for 18 minutes.
cues.zh: 先说明一下这意味着什么：如果电厂里的操作员站在每小时800雷姆的辐射场中，20秒内就会达到他们一年允许的最大辐射剂量。第一次辐射警报响起后，值班人员基本上一直不愿承认电厂状态和堆芯损伤。但这次警报响起时，这是最严重的那种。警报刚响过，他们终于决定重新开启高压注入。但他们只让它运行了18分钟。

cues.en: because it causes the water level in the pressurizer to rise. They are so fixated on the pressurizer. It wasn't until 826 in the morning, four hours and 26 minutes after the start of the accident, after the situation continued to worsen, that they finally decide to re-enable high-pressure injection and leave it on. And they do this largely out of desperation. They're not sure what else to try at this point to get control of the plant. It would take until 1030 in the morning for these thousand gallon per minute pumps to cover the core with water.
cues.zh: 因为这会让稳压器水位上升。他们太执着于稳压器了。直到早上8:26，也就是事故开始后4小时26分钟，在情况持续恶化之后，他们才终于决定重新开启高压注入并保持运行。他们这么做很大程度上是出于绝望。此时他们也不知道还能试什么来控制电厂。直到早上10:30，这些每分钟1000加仑的泵才把堆芯用水覆盖。

cues.en: ending the primary accident sequence. Over the next few days, there would be continued worry about a radiation release at the plant, and so they'd keep monitoring the situation on the ground. They'd send teams around the perimeter of the plant with radiation detectors. They flew them overhead in helicopters. But the redundant containment in the plant did its job. No significant radiation release would ever occur. There's a lot of public worry about a potential hydrogen explosion, because when the zirconium cladding of the fuel rod melts, it reacts with the coolant to produce hydrogen.
cues.zh: 结束了主事故序列。接下来几天，人们持续担心电厂发生辐射释放，因此一直监测现场情况。他们派携带辐射探测器的队伍绕电厂周边巡查，还用直升机载他们在上空飞行监测。但电厂的多重安全壳发挥了作用。始终没有发生重大辐射释放。公众非常担心可能发生氢气爆炸，因为燃料棒的锆包壳熔化时会与冷却剂反应产生氢气。

cues.en: But it turns out that public fear was fueled largely by incorrect calculations. There wasn't nearly as much hydrogen released as people were afraid there was. On Sunday, April 1st, four days after the accident, President Jimmy Carter and his wife Rosalyn would visit the plant, tour the control room, to reassure the American public about the safety of nuclear power, and to reassure them that the situation at Three Mile Island was well under control.
cues.zh: 但事实证明，公众的恐惧很大程度上是由错误计算煽动起来的。释放出的氢气远没有人们担心的那么多。在事故发生四天后的4月1日星期日，美国总统吉米·卡特和夫人罗莎琳将访问该电厂，参观控制室，以向美国公众保证核电的安全性，并让他们确信三里岛的情况完全在控制之中。

cues.en: He would later convene an investigatory commission that would result in this report on the accident that I've drawn a lot of the facts for this talk today from. Three Mile Island Unit 2 would be written off as a total loss. A $500 million investment completely written off three months after it began operation. About 20 tons of melted uranium ended up at the bottom of the core. Another 10 tons is blobbed together there in the middle. This is what they found when they began the initial cleanup in 1983.
cues.zh: 他后来召集了一个调查委员会，并出台了这份关于事故的报告，我今天演讲的很多事实都取材于此。三里岛2号机组被宣告彻底报废。刚投运三个月，5亿美元的投资就彻底打了水漂。大约20吨熔化的铀最终落到了堆芯底部。另有10吨则凝结在中间。这就是他们在1983年开始初步清理时发现的情况。

cues.en: You're looking at severed melted fuel rods that ended up at the bottom of the reactor the final cost of the initial cleanup Just over one billion dollars and it took 14 years and they're still not done Three Mile Island unit 2 is still standing in the middle of the Susquehanna River You can see unit 1 here on your right. It's still operating. It's still producing electricity Final cleanup of unit 2 won't take place until unit 1 is decommissioned and that's currently scheduled to take place in 2034
cues.zh: 你看到的是断裂并熔化的燃料棒，它们最终落在了反应堆底部。初步清理的最终成本略超10亿美元，历时14年，而且他们还没完工。三里岛2号机组仍然矗立在萨斯quehanna河中央。你可以在右边看到1号机组。它仍在运行。它仍在发电。2号机组的最终清理工作要等到1号机组退役后才会进行，目前计划于2034年进行。

cues.en: So what happened? How did these four men miss so many signs along the way that their reactor was in the middle of a loss of coolant accident? Why didn't they just leave the emergency core cooling system on when it activated? Why didn't they close the block valve sooner? Sidney Decker, in his book, The Field Guide to Understanding Human Error, introduces the concept of first stories and second stories. And the story I've just told you of Three Mile Island is a first story, intentionally so. First stories focus on the humans in the story.
cues.zh: 那么究竟发生了什么？这四个人怎么会一路错过那么多迹象，没发现他们的反应堆正处于失水事故中？为什么应急堆芯冷却系统启动时，他们不让它继续开着？为什么他们没有早点关闭隔离阀？西德尼·德克在他的《理解人为错误的现场指南》一书中，引入了第一故事和第二故事的概念。我刚才给你讲的三里岛的故事就是一个第一故事，而且是刻意为之的。第一故事聚焦于故事中的人类。

cues.en: and what they should have done differently. A first story inevitably lays blame for the accident at the feet of the humans involved and the decisions they made. This is problematic for a couple of reasons. There's a couple of biases that we all have. The first is hindsight bias. It turns out that when you review an event after it's occurred and you know the outcome, you automatically exaggerate your own ability to have predicted and prevented that outcome. This is known sometimes as the I saw it all along effect.
cues.zh: 以及他们本应有哪些不同的做法。第一个故事不可避免地把事故归咎于涉事人员及其所做的决定。这有几个问题。我们都有几种偏见。第一种是后见之明偏误。事实证明，当你在事件发生后回顾并已知结果时，你会自动夸大自己预测和阻止该结果的能力。这有时被称为“我早就看出来了”效应。

cues.en: An example of that here is all that water in the sump had to be coming from somewhere. I know nothing about nuclear reactors, and I would have figured out that there was a leak. The second is outcome bias. It turns out that once you know the outcome of a situation, you carry the full weight of that outcome into evaluating every decision that led to it. It makes you more willing to judge those decisions, and it makes you more likely to judge them harshly. A good example here is that knowing the outcome of this is a partial meltdown,
cues.zh: 这里的一个例子是，油槽里的水必定来自某处。我对核反应堆一无所知，但我本应推断出有泄漏。第二种是结果偏误。事实证明，一旦你知道情况的结果，你就会把该结果的全部影响带入对导致该结果的每一个决定的评估中。这让你更愿意评判那些决定，也更可能严厉地评判它们。一个很好的例子是，知道这次是部分堆芯熔毁的结果，

cues.en: Turning off the emergency core cooling system early in the accident looks like a really moronic decision. So what should we do instead? We should look for the second story. There's always a second story buried under that first story. In a second story, human error is seen as an effect of systemic vulnerabilities deeper inside the organization. Not a result of bad decision-making or failure to follow instructions. So how do we get to a second story? We have to dig into decisions from the perspective of the people who made those decisions.
cues.zh: 在事故早期关闭应急堆芯冷却系统看起来是个非常愚蠢的决定。那么我们应该怎么做？我们应该寻找第二个故事。在第一个故事之下总有一个第二个故事。在第二个故事中，人为错误被视为组织内部更深层系统性漏洞的影响，而不是糟糕决策或未遵循指示的结果。那么我们如何找到第二个故事？我们必须从做出决定的人的角度深入探究这些决定。

cues.en: We have to try to see the world through their eyes. We have to work to consider the messy reality that they were facing when they made the decision, not the clean room conditions that your hindsight gives you. And we have to look through the lens of positive intent, with the belief that everyone involved made the best decisions they could with the information they had. So let's see if we can find some second stories from Three Mile Island. Let's start early in the sequence. Why in the world did Fred Shimon make the call to turn off the emergency core cooling system five minutes into the accident? We'll find our answer.
cues.zh: 我们必须尝试通过他们的视角来看待这个世界。我们必须努力去思考他们做决定时面对的混乱现实，而不是你事后诸葛亮带来的无菌室般的理想条件。而且我们必须带着善意的视角去看待，相信所有相关人员都根据他们当时掌握的信息做出了最好的决定。所以，让我们看看能否从三里岛事件中找到一些不同的视角。让我们从事件序列的早期开始。弗雷德·希蒙（Fred Shimon）到底为什么在事故发生五分钟时决定关闭紧急堆芯冷却系统？我们会找到答案的。

cues.en: in the pressurizer. In his deposition to the presidential inquiry, Fred Scheman says that he turned off the emergency core cooling system because it was causing the water level in the pressurizer to rise, and he was afraid that the pressurizer was going to, quote, go solid, unquote. And that's a phrase that appears throughout this deposition. This whole crew was worried about the pressurizer going solid. So what does that mean? Well, remember that one of the pressurizer's key jobs is to absorb pressure shocks to the system. Letting it go solid is to let it fill up with water.
cues.zh: 在稳压器里。在其向总统调查委员会的陈述中，弗雷德·舍曼（Fred Scheman）表示，他关闭紧急堆芯冷却系统是因为它导致稳压器里的水位上升，他担心稳压器会——引述他的话说——“变实”（go solid）。这是一个贯穿整份陈述的短语。整个机组人员都担心稳压器会“变实”。那么这是什么意思呢？记住，稳压器的一个核心工作就是吸收系统的压力冲击。让它“变实”就是让它充满水，

cues.en: to the point that it can no longer absorb those pressure shocks. So that makes sense. He doesn't want the pressurizer to go solid, but he has to know that the core is in danger. Why does his concern for the pressurizer override his concern for the core? Well, that answer goes all the way back to Admiral Hyman Rickover in the early days of the nuclear navy. It turns out that Bill Zewe, Fred Scheman, Ed Frederick, and Craig Faust were all former naval nuclear reactors. In the naval reactor training designed by Admiral Rickover,
cues.zh: 直到它再也无法吸收这些压力冲击。所以这说得通。他不想让稳压器“变实”，但他一定知道堆芯正处于危险之中。为什么他对稳压器的担忧会压倒他对堆芯的担忧呢？这个答案要追溯到核海军早期的海曼·里克高弗（Hyman Rickover）海军上将。原来，比尔·泽韦（Bill Zewe）、弗雷德·舍曼、埃德·弗雷德里克（Ed Frederick）和克雷格·福斯特（Craig Faust）都曾是海军核反应堆操作员。在里克高弗海军上将设计的海军反应堆培训中，

cues.en: had drilled into these, man, that keeping the pressurizer from going solid was the single most important job of a nuclear reactor operator. That actually makes sense on a submarine. The reason is that a 1960s-era submarine produces 12 megawatts of thermal energy for its propulsion. Three Mile Island Unit 2, in order to make 906 megawatts of electricity because of inefficiencies in the system, has to produce 2,841 megawatts of heat. That's a lot of heat.
cues.zh: 已经向这些人反复灌输过，防止稳压器“变实”是核反应堆操作员最最重要的工作。这在潜水艇上其实是说得通的。原因是一艘 20 世纪 60 年代产的潜水艇为其推进产生 12 兆瓦的热能。而三里岛核电站 2 号机组为了产生 906 兆瓦的电力，由于系统效率低下，必须产生 2,841 兆瓦的热量。那是相当多的热量。

cues.en: Remember that when you scram a reactor, the primary heat production stops immediately, but there's still decay heat going on, and it takes a while for that decay heat to cool down. In a submarine reactor, that decay heat is trivial. It's about 780 kilowatts. You can essentially just ignore it. If the reactor was completely uncovered, this would not be enough heat to do any damage. In a power reactor, that 6.5% of decay heat is 185 megawatts of heat. If you don't continually carry that heat away,
cues.zh: 请记住，当你紧急关闭反应堆时，主要的热量产生会立即停止，但仍然会有衰变热持续产生，这些衰变热需要一段时间才能冷却下来。在潜艇反应堆中，这种衰变热微不足道。它大约是 780 千瓦。你基本上可以忽略它。如果反应堆完全暴露在外，这点热量也不足以造成任何破坏。但在发电反应堆中，这 6.5% 的衰变热相当于 1.85 亿瓦的热量。如果你不持续把这些热量带走，

cues.en: it will cause damage to the fuel. In a submarine, a water hammer with no shock absorption is literally the worst-case scenario where it could result in a loss of propulsion and a disabled ship. Carrying that mentality into the operation of a power reactor where far worse things are possible is a huge systemic vulnerability, one that was unrealized before the Three Mile Island accident. And so Fred Shima, faced with a rising pressurizer, inferred that the system was full of water already.
cues.zh: 这会对燃料造成损害。在潜艇中，没有减震装置的水锤现象简直是最坏的情况，可能导致推进力丧失和舰艇瘫痪。将这种心态带入核反应堆的运行中——那里可能发生更糟糕的事情——是一个巨大的系统性漏洞，这在三哩岛事故之前从未被意识到。因此，弗雷德·希马面对上升的稳压器水位，推断系统已经充满了水。

cues.en: Allowing the emergency core cooling system to continue high-pressure injection would overfill the system, risking a full pressurizer, and so, in an effort to keep the reactor safe, he turned off emergency core cooling. Let's look at another one. Why did Bill Zeween not close the block valve when he first checked the outlet pipe temperature? If you'll remember, the reported outlet temperature was 228 degrees Fahrenheit, and the procedures of the plant called for the block valve to be shut if it's anything over 200 degrees. But it turns out...
cues.zh:
允许紧急堆芯冷却系统继续进行高压注入会使系统过度灌满，从而导致加压器满液的风险，因此，为了保障反应堆的安全，他关闭了紧急堆芯冷却。

cues.en: that at 3 Mile Island Unit 2, the pilot-operated relief valve had been leaking almost since the first day of operation. Very small leak, just a little bit of steam, and it was such an insignificant issue that it actually wouldn't be fixed until the first refueling shut down. The consequences of that leak were that the outlet temperature of the pilot-operated relief valve was regularly over 200 degrees Fahrenheit, on an almost daily basis.
cues.zh: 三哩岛2号机组那个先导式安全阀，几乎从运行第一天起就在漏了。很小的泄漏，只是一点点蒸汽，问题小到直到第一次换料停机才会去修。这个泄漏的后果是，先导式安全阀的出口温度经常超过200华氏度，几乎每天都是如此。

cues.en: And so Bill Z, we had been conditioned that seeing temperatures above 200 degrees, despite what the reactor operation manual said, were okay. And when he evaluated that temperature, he thought about it in terms of, well, the pilot-operated relief valve was just venting really hot water. It's normally about 200 degrees. 228 doesn't seem unreasonable to me. So that's part of it. The other part is when he looked at the control panel to check the position of the pilot-operated relief valve, he saw that it was green, indicating the valve was closed.
cues.zh: 于是Bill Z，我们已经习惯了看到200度以上的温度，尽管反应堆操作手册上不是这么说的，我们觉得没问题。当他评估那个温度时，他的想法是，先导式安全阀只是在排放很热的水。正常大约200度，228看起来也不算离谱。这是一部分原因。另一部分是，当他看控制面板检查先导式安全阀的位置时，他看到是绿色的，表示阀门关闭。

cues.en: But that's not actually what that light meant. The light on the control panel only indicated the signal that had been sent to the valve by the computer. A green light simply meant that the computer had told the valve to close. It was not coupled to the physical position of the valve. The only way to know the actual position of the pilot-operated relief valve was to infer it from the outlet temperature. And so Bill Zewe, assimilating all the information that he had at his disposal, and considering the full pressurizer...
cues.zh: 但那盏灯实际上并不是这个意思。控制面板上的灯只表示计算机发给阀门的信号。绿灯只意味着计算机告诉阀门关闭。它和阀门的实际位置没有关联。要知道先导式安全阀的真实位置，唯一的办法是从出口温度去推断。于是Bill Zewe综合了他手头所有的信息，并考虑了完整的稳压器……

cues.en: left the block valve open so the pilot-operated relief valve could still respond if there was a pressure spike. He left the valve open to keep the reactor safe. One more, this is a quick one, I promise. How did the crew miss the significance of the sump alarm? That much water in the sump is obvious. How did they not know they had a coolant leak? And the answer is really simple. They never got the alarm. The control room at Three Mile Island relayed alarm conditions to the crew in two ways. Number one is this row of lights on the wall, and there's a corresponding row on the other side.
cues.zh: 他把截止阀开着，以便在压力激增时，先导式安全阀仍能响应。他把阀门开着是为了确保反应堆的安全。还有一个，这个很快，我保证。机组人员怎么会忽视集水坑警报的重要性？集水坑里有那么多水，这显而易见。他们怎么会不知道自己遇到了冷却剂泄漏？答案其实很简单。他们根本没收到警报。三里岛的控制室通过两种方式向机组人员传达警报状态。第一种就是墙上这排灯，另一侧也有一排对应的灯。

cues.en: About 600 alarm lights in total. And on a given day, when the plant is running exactly as it's designed, 40 to 50 of these would be on. They're very noisy. There's also no rhyme or reason to where they're placed. One of the most important alarm lights in the entire system, the reactor pressure alarm, is right next to a light that indicates that the elevator in the containment building is stuck. The third problem with these is they don't indicate any chronology. You can't tell by looking at them when an alarm turned on.
cues.zh: 总共大约有 600 个警报灯。在某一天，当电厂完全按设计运行常态时，其中会有 40 到 50 个亮着。它们非常吵。而且它们的放置位置也毫无逻辑可言。整个系统中最重要的警报灯之一——反应堆压力警报灯，正好挨着一个指示安全壳内电梯卡住的灯。它们的第三个问题是，它们不显示任何时间顺序。你没法通过观察它们来判断警报是什么时候触发的。

cues.en: and what's new since the last time you looked at the panel. They did have an answer for that one. They had an alarm printer. Every time an alarm would go off, this printer would print a line describing the alarm. The problem is, it's connected to the computer by a 300 baud serial connection. Very, very slow. And so less than an hour into the accident, after more than 100 alarms have gone off, it would take the printer two and a half hours to finish printing all the alarms.
cues.zh: 以及自你上次查看面板以来有什么新情况。他们确实找到了解决这个问题的办法。他们有一个警报打印机。每当警报响起，这台打印机就会打印出一行描述警报的文字。问题是，它通过一个 300 波特的串行连接连到计算机上。非常非常慢。因此，在事故发生不到一小时后，在有一百多个警报响起之后，打印机需要两个半小时才能打印完所有的警报。

cues.en: So there's no way the operators can keep up with the flood of information that's being directed at them. And so they just don't see the sump alarm. They don't get the message that the sump is full. So how do we implement this idea of first and second stories with our teams? Dr. Decker has some helpful advice for us. First, when we're trying to figure out why something went wrong, we agree on a baseline rule that human error is never the cause. Human error is always a symptom of underlying systemic problems or problem.
cues.zh: 所以操作员根本没法跟上涌向他们的海量信息，于是就看不见集水坑的警报，收不到集水坑已满的消息。那么，我们如何在团队中落实第一故事和第二故事的理念呢？Decker博士给了我们一些有用的建议。首先，当我们试图弄清某件事为何出错时，我们要约定一条底线规则：人为失误绝不是原因。人为失误始终是深层系统性问题或问题的症状。

cues.en: So blaming an issue on human error keeps us from figuring out what really went wrong. A good way of helping frame the conversation in these terms is to ask what is responsible for an outcome, not whose fault it is. Second principle is to understand why it made sense. The people on your teams don't come to work intending to do a bad job. Chances are, when they make a decision that you don't understand, they had a very good reason why they did it. Take the time to see the world through their eyes and understand why their decision made sense.
cues.zh: 所以，把问题归咎于人为失误，会让我们无法查明真正出错的原因。帮助大家用这种视角展开讨论的一个好方法，是问“是什么导致了这个结果”，而不是“是谁的错”。第二条原则是理解它当时为什么合理。你团队里的人上班时并不是打算把工作做砸。很可能，当他们做出一个你不理解的决定时，他们是有充分理由的。花点时间从他们的角度看世界，理解他们的决定为什么合理。

cues.en: Third, seek forward accountability, not backwards. Our instinct when things go wrong is often to figure out who's responsible and punish them. When we try to move our organizations away from blame and towards finding second stories, one of the most common objections is, but what about holding people accountable? Turns out that removing punishment actually frees people up to candidly share their stories of what happened so you can learn from them instead of those experiences getting swept under the rug.
cues.zh: 第三，追求向前问责，而不是向后追责。事情出错时，我们的本能往往是找出责任人并加以惩罚。当我们试图让组织摆脱指责、转向寻找第二故事时，最常见的反对意见之一就是：那还怎么让人承担责任？事实证明，取消惩罚反而能让人坦诚地讲出事情经过，让你从中学习，而不是让这些经历被掩盖过去。

cues.en: If you've implemented blameless postmortems in your organization, you've seen this. But there's another part of this that's very important, and it's not talked about very often. The act of telling the story of what happened, of giving their account and owning their part in it, is generally all the accountability that well-intentioned people need to improve. They're already beating themselves up for the decision that they made. They're already upset that something bad has happened.
cues.zh: 如果你在团队中推行过免责事后复盘，你就见过这种情况。但其中还有一个非常重要的部分，却很少被提及。讲述事情经过、陈述事实并承担自己那部分责任，对于心地善良的人来说，这通常就是改进所需的全部问责。他们已经为自己做出的决定而自责了。他们已经为发生了糟糕的事情而感到难过了。

cues.en: They don't need systemic blame and punishment. They don't need shame. It doesn't help anybody. It just teaches them not to share what happened and try to hide it. Backwards accountability looks to blame somebody for past events. Forward accountability seeks to help people tell the story of what happened and come to terms with it, and focus on the work necessary for change and improvement going forward. The beauty of this technique is that it's so broadly applicable. There's always a second story if you're willing to do the work to find it.
cues.zh: 他们不需要系统性的指责和惩罚。他们不需要羞辱。这对任何人都没有帮助。这只会教导他们隐瞒真相、不再分享发生了什么。向后问责是为了将过去事件的责任归咎于某人。向前问责则是为了帮助人们讲述事情经过并正视它，专注于未来变革和改进所必需的工作。这种技术的妙处在于它的适用范围非常广泛。如果你愿意花心思去寻找，总会有第二个故事。

cues.en: This will work when somebody drops the production database. It'll work when your team misses an important deadline. It'll work when a key team member chooses to leave. It'll even work when sales misses their quarterly sales goal. It requires honesty and building trust, but it's worth it because finding the second story is such a powerful way for your team to grow and improve. And it allows you to treat your teammates with the humanity that they deserve. It goes back to the psychological safety that Julia was talking about earlier. This is a great way to build psychological safety in your team.
cues.zh: 当有人搞砸了生产数据库时，这管用。当你的团队错过重要截止日期时，这管用。当核心团队成员选择离开时，这管用。甚至当销售部门未达成季度销售目标时，这也管用。这需要诚实和建立信任，但这是值得的，因为找到第二个故事是帮助团队成长和进步的强大方式。它能让你以队友应有的人性去对待他们。这就回到了茱莉之前谈到的心理安全感。这是在团队中建立心理安全感的绝佳方法。

cues.en: It turns out that who destroyed Three Mile Island is not a fair question at all. The question we should be asking is what destroyed Three Mile Island? And thankfully, that's the question that the President's Commission asked. Check out the subtitle of their report. This report is full of second stories. And those second stories revealed weaknesses in reactor design and operator training throughout the nuclear industry worldwide. By getting past human error,
cues.zh: 事实证明，追问“是谁毁了三里岛”根本就不是一个恰当的问题。我们真正该问的是：是什么毁了三里岛？所幸，总统委员会问的正是这个问题。看看他们报告的副标题。这份报告充满了第二层故事。而这些第二层故事揭示了全球核工业在反应堆设计和操作员培训方面的弱点。通过超越人为失误，

cues.en: to the real causes of the accident at Three Mile Island, the President's Commission made the world a safer place. If you take the time to find the second stories for everything that happens, not just your outages, you'll make your organization a safer place for the people who work there, and you'll fix the things that impact your delivery speed and quality. Best of luck.
cues.zh: 深挖三里岛事故的真正根源，总统委员会让世界变得更安全了。如果你愿意花时间去挖掘每件事背后的第二层故事，而不只是你的系统故障，你就会让你的组织对在那里工作的人来说更安全，你也会修复那些影响交付速度和交付质量的问题。祝你好运。
